newsitem.title: UK: Windfall building society gains could fuel UK boom.
newsitem.headline: Windfall building society gains could fuel UK boom.

text.p: Britain could be pushed into a mini-boom if consumers spend only a quarter of the estimated 22 billion pound ($36 billion) windfall payments they are set to receive from building societies, analysts said on Monday.
"There is a little bit more caution that there was in the 1980s but there are still strong risks. The scenario is mini-boom/mini-bust," said Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International.
Millions of Britons will get one-off share payments from building societies which are converting themselves into banks or merging with other building societies.

Analysts fear consumers could simply go on a spending spree with the proceeds -- a concern underlined after the shares of former building society Alliance and Leicester soared in price following their flotation on Monday.
The consequences could be dramatic. The size of the handout could amount to the equivalent of a 10 pence cut off Britain's basic 23 percent rate of income tax for one year.
"We could be well on the way to a mini-consumption boom --nearly as bad as the late 1980s," said Ruth Lea, head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors.
The late 1980s boom under then Chancellor of the Exchequer Nigel Lawson led to the longest recession since the second world war.
The government failed to recognise signs that the economy was overheating and that borrowing was out of control -- a state in part fuelled by reductions in the top rates of income tax.
The Conservative government -- which faces an election on May 1 -- is confident that most of the building society payments will be saved.
But analysts are dubious and say anecdotal evidence suggests that a sizeable chunk will find its way into the shops.

An indication of consumers' hunger for cash came from reports that members of Alliance and Leicester were selling a hefty 27 percent of the total number of their free shares, pocketing fat profits after the price rocketed to 571.5 pence.
Moreover, five years of economic growth are dulling the memory of the 1990-92 recession and the pain of losses in Britain's residential housing market has been eased by rising prices.
"We are certainly aware of retailers increasing their stock in the hopes of benefitting from some sort of surge in spending," SBC-Warburg economist Darren Winder said.
"At the moment, uncertainty about the outcome of the election is probably dampening consumer confidence. We won't get a clear picture until after it's out of the way."
Analysts say that whoever wins the election will have to tighten monetary and ideally fiscal policy if the errors of the late 1980s are to be avoided.

Both the ruling Conservatives and the opposition Labour party, heavily tipped by opinion polls to form the next government, are pledged to free Britain from the stop/go cycle which has dogged its economy since the 1960s.
But they need to act soon. Average earnings are on the increase, unemployment is dropping and the feelgood factor which sparked a borrowing orgy in the late 1980s is creeping back.
Windfall gains could be the last straw.
"This is adding liquidity to the economy in a serious way," Winder said, arguing the payments would simply drive prices higher without increasing tangible wealth.
Britain's 6.0 percent official interest rates are expected to be increased by 1/4 or 1/2 a percentage point immediately after the election to rein in demand.

But there will have to be an additional fiscal drain of some four billion pounds if the government is to have any chance of getting and keeping inflation inside the offical target range of 2.5 percent or lower and controlling official borrowing.
"We are pretty close to the target but the question is sustainability," said IBJ's Hannah.

"We've also got to recognise that the European benchmarks are improving all the time -- some of them are under 2.0 percent while we're still struggling with 2.5." UK core inflation was 2.7 percent in March.

Labour has said it will hold a budget shortly after taking power and analysts say this would be an ideal opportunity to raise extra revenue. But the party has already ruled out the most straightforward option -- increasing income tax.
Instead a range of lower profile measures are likely, including scrapping tax relief on mortgages.
"The UK will have to endure a period of slower economic growth but I would have thought Labour would have learnt from the mistakes of the Conservatives," SBC's Winder said.
"They tried to put the whole burden on interest rates and found they had to raise taxes later. I think they're paying for that now," he said. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
